e-602.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
e-602.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/834eff403ac2a6f696e104ec914cac1b951f8a6d989e11c0e9f2576ac9e7f0d8.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].
$$
e-602.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{({t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-7130.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
e-7130.problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
e-7130.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

e-603.knowledge_point: Finding the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
e-603.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)
e-603.worked_solution:
Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The arc length is ∫₀¹√((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²) dt. Here dx/dt=3t²+2t and dy/dt=3t²−2t, so their squared sum is 18t⁴+8t². Since t≥0, the integrand simplifies to t√(18t²+8), giving option d.

after.problem:

$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2}+2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{18{t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\sqrt{18{t}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3+t2,y=t3−t2 from t=0 to t=1 ?

a
2∫01t9t2+2t+4dt
b
2∫01t3t2+2dt
c
∫01t18t2+24t+8dt
d
∫01t18t2+8dt
e
∫01t9t2+4dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3+t2)=3t2+2t and dydt=ddt(t3−t2)=3t2−2t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫01(3t2+2t)2+(3t2−2t)2dt=∫019t4+12t3+4t2+9t4−12t3+4t2dt=∫0118t4+8t2dt=∫01t18t2+8dt.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d. The derivatives are 3t²+2t and 3t²−2t; their squared sum is 18t⁴+8t². Since t≥0 on [0,1], its square root is t√(18t²+8). The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-{t}^{2}$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})=3{t}^{2}-2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2}+2t)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{2}-2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}-12{t}^{3}+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{18{t}^{4}+8{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\sqrt{18{t}^{2}+8}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3+1,y=3t from t=−2 to t=0 (shown above)?

a
3∫−20t2+3dt
b
∫−203t4+1dt
c
∫−20t4+3dt
d
3∫−20t2+1dt
e
3∫−20t4+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Using the parametric arc-length formula, dx/dt=3t² and dy/dt=3. Thus the speed is √(9t⁴+9)=3√(t⁴+1). Integrating from −2 to 0 gives option e.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/120220c7c1a24c68c1a9282548efcf62c34fd110bd11911799a2a83409f257ab.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+1,\,y=3t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=0$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3+1,y=3t from t=−2 to t=0 (shown above)?

a
3∫−20t2+3dt
b
∫−203t4+1dt
c
∫−20t4+3dt
d
3∫−20t2+1dt
e
3∫−20t4+1dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3+1)=3t2 and dydt=ddt(3t)=3.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−20(3t2)2+(3)2dt=∫−209t4+9dt=3∫−20t4+1dt.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/120220c7c1a24c68c1a9282548efcf62c34fd110bd11911799a2a83409f257ab.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}+1,\,y=3t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=0$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{-2}^{0}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+1}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−1,y=t2−t from t=0 to t=1 ?

a
 ∫013t2+2t−1dt
b
 ∫019t4+4t2−4t+1dt
c
 ∫019t4+2t2−2t+1dt
d
 ∫01t2−12t+1dt
e
 ∫013t4+4t2−2t+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: For parametric arc length, integrate √((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²). Here dx/dt=3t² and dy/dt=2t−1, so the squared speed is 9t⁴+(2t−1)²=9t⁴+4t²−4t+1. This gives option b.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-1,\,y={t}^{2}-t$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}-4t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−1,y=t2−t from t=0 to t=1 ?

a
 ∫013t2+2t−1dt
b
 ∫019t4+4t2−4t+1dt
c
 ∫019t4+2t2−2t+1dt
d
 ∫01t2−12t+1dt
e
 ∫013t4+4t2−2t+1dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3−1)=3t2 and dydt=ddt(t2−t)=2t−1.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫01(3t2)2+(2t−1)2dt=∫019t4+4t2−4t+1dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b: dx/dt=3t² and dy/dt=2t−1, so (dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²=9t⁴+4t²−4t+1. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-1,\,y={t}^{2}-t$
from $t=0$ to $t=1$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(2t-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+4{t}^{2}-4t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t−1,y=t2+2 from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−121+4t2dt
b
∫−124+4t+t2dt
c
∫−12t+4t2dt
d
∫−124+t+4t2dt
e
∫−121+4t+4t2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are dx/dt=1 and dy/dt=2t. The arc length is therefore the integral from −1 to 2 of √(1²+(2t)²)=√(1+4t²), which matches option a.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t-1,\,y={t}^{2}+2$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2)=2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t−1,y=t2+2 from t=−1 to t=2 ?

a
∫−121+4t2dt
b
∫−124+4t+t2dt
c
∫−12t+4t2dt
d
∫−124+t+4t2dt
e
∫−121+4t+4t2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t−1)=1 and dydt=ddt(t2+2)=2t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−12(1)2+(2t)2dt=∫−121+4t2dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t-1,\,y={t}^{2}+2$
from $t=-1$ to $t=2$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2)=2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(2t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−8,y=t4+5t from t=−2 to t=3 ?

a
∫−2316t6+9t4+40t3+25dt
b
∫−2316t6+49t4+25dt
c
3∫−23t6+t4+t3+25dt
d
∫−234t6+3t4+4t3+5dt
e
2∫−238t6+9t4+20t3+25dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are dx/dt=3t² and dy/dt=4t³+5. Their squared sum is 9t⁴+(4t³+5)²=16t⁶+9t⁴+40t³+25. Integrating its square root from −2 to 3 gives option a.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-8,\,y={t}^{4}+5t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=3$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-8)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+5t)=4{t}^{3}+5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(4{t}^{3}+5)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+16{t}^{6}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t3−8,y=t4+5t from t=−2 to t=3 ?

a
∫−2316t6+9t4+40t3+25dt
b
∫−2316t6+49t4+25dt
c
3∫−23t6+t4+t3+25dt
d
∫−234t6+3t4+4t3+5dt
e
2∫−238t6+9t4+20t3+25dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t3−8)=3t2 and dydt=ddt(t4+5t)=4t3+5.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫−23(3t2)2+(4t3+5)2dt=∫−239t4+16t6+40t3+25dt=∫−2316t6+9t4+40t3+25dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-8,\,y={t}^{4}+5t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=3$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-8)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+5t)=4{t}^{3}+5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(4{t}^{3}+5)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+16{t}^{6}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t),y=t−sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π4 ?

a
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)+cos⁡(t)−cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=cos(t)+sin(t) and y′(t)=1−cos(t). Their squared sum is 1+sin(2t)+1−2cos(t)+cos²(t)=2+sin(2t)−2cos(t)+cos²(t). Integrating its square root from 0 to π/4 gives option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t),y=t−sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π4 ?

a
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
d
∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)+cos⁡(t)−cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t))=cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t) and dydt=ddt(t−sin⁡(t))=1−cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/4(cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t))2+(1−cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/4cos2⁡(t)+sin2⁡(t)+2cos⁡(t)sin⁡(t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))^{2}+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(sin⁡(t)−cos⁡(t))=cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t) and dydt=ddt(t−sin⁡(t))=1−cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/4(cos⁡(t)+sin⁡(t))2+(1−cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/4cos2⁡(t)+sin2⁡(t)+2cos⁡(t)sin⁡(t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/41+sin⁡(2t)+1+cos2⁡(t)−2cos⁡(t)dt=∫0π/42+sin⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(t)+cos2⁡(t)dt.

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(3t),y=3sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/23sin2⁡(t)+cos2⁡(3t)dt
c
3∫0π/22sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
d
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
e
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(t)+cos2⁡(3t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=−3sin(3t) and y′(t)=3cos(t). Thus the speed is √(9sin²(3t)+9cos²(t))=3√(sin²(3t)+cos²(t)). Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/d683c3960705fa32d11826008a9844c51c8e59e38f5158fce7f4e44c31b97ca9.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(3t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(3t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(3t),y=3sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/23sin2⁡(t)+cos2⁡(3t)dt
c
3∫0π/22sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
d
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt
e
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(t)+cos2⁡(3t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡(3t))=−3sin⁡(3t) and dydt=ddt(3sin⁡(t))=3cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(−3sin⁡(3t))2+(3cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/29sin2⁡(3t)+9cos2⁡(t)dt=3∫0π/2sin2⁡(3t)+cos2⁡(t)dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. The derivatives are −3sin(3t) and 3cos(t), giving speed 3√(sin²(3t)+cos²(t)). Integrate this from 0 to π/2. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/d683c3960705fa32d11826008a9844c51c8e59e38f5158fce7f4e44c31b97ca9.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t),\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(3t)+9{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(3t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=2sin⁡(3t)−1,y=2cos⁡(2t)+2 from t=0 to t=π2 ?

a
2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)−2sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
4∫0π/2cos2⁡(3t)+sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)−4sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)+2sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=6cos(3t) and y′(t)=−4sin(2t). Thus the speed is √(36cos²(3t)+16sin²(2t))=2√(9cos²(3t)+4sin²(2t)). Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives option a.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=2sin⁡(3t)−1,y=2cos⁡(2t)+2 from t=0 to t=π2 ?

a
2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)−2sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
4∫0π/2cos2⁡(3t)+sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)−4sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
2∫0π/26cos2⁡(3t)+2sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(2sin⁡(3t)−1)=2cos⁡(3t)⋅3=6cos⁡(3t) and dydt=ddt(2cos⁡(2t)+2)=−2sin⁡(2t)⋅2=−4sin⁡(2t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(6cos⁡(3t))2+(−4sin⁡(2t))2dt=∫0π/236cos2⁡(3t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt=2∫0π/29cos2⁡(3t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1,\,y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}

To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\cdot 3 \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2 \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))^{2}+(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{36{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡(3t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(5t),y=6sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
2∫0π/25sin2⁡(5t)+6cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/225sin⁡(t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/225sin⁡(5t)+36cos⁡(6t)dt
d
∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/210sin2⁡(5t)+12cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=−5sin(5t) and y′(t)=6cos(t). Arc length integrates √((x′)²+(y′)²), so the integrand is √(25sin²(5t)+36cos²(t)). With limits 0 to π/2, this matches option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/8868658c9bc7195f435a0109fce26b8a4fa39324c0a9a39e3fb644c5f02cdc9b.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡(5t)+36{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=cos⁡(5t),y=6sin⁡(t) from t=0 to t=π2 (shown above)?

a
2∫0π/25sin2⁡(5t)+6cos2⁡(t)dt
b
∫0π/225sin⁡(t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
c
∫0π/225sin⁡(5t)+36cos⁡(6t)dt
d
∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt
e
∫0π/210sin2⁡(5t)+12cos2⁡(t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡(5t))=−5sin⁡(5t) and dydt=ddt(6sin⁡(t))=6cos⁡(t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π/2(−5sin⁡(5t))2+(6cos⁡(t))2dt=∫0π/225sin2⁡(5t)+36cos2⁡(t)dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d: x′(t)=−5sin(5t) and y′(t)=6cos(t), so the speed is √(25sin²(5t)+36cos²(t)). Integrating from 0 to π/2 gives the arc length. The incorrect feedback concerns the deliberately submitted option b.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/8868658c9bc7195f435a0109fce26b8a4fa39324c0a9a39e3fb644c5f02cdc9b.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown above)?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡(5t)+36{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t+2sin⁡(t),y=1+cos⁡(2t) from t=2 to t=5 ?

a
∫251+4cos⁡(t)+4cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
∫251+2cos⁡(t)+2cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
∫251+2cos⁡(t)+16cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫251+8cos⁡(t)+16cos2⁡(t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫251+4cos⁡(t)+4cos2⁡(t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′(t)=1+2cos(t) and y′(t)=−2sin(2t). Their squared sum is 1+4cos(t)+4cos²(t)+4sin²(2t). Integrating its square root from 2 to 5 gives option a.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$
from $t=2$ to $t=5$ ?
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}

Question 10

Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations x=t+2sin⁡(t),y=1+cos⁡(2t) from t=2 to t=5 ?

a
∫251+4cos⁡(t)+4cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
b
∫251+2cos⁡(t)+2cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
c
∫251+2cos⁡(t)+16cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt
d
∫251+8cos⁡(t)+16cos2⁡(t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫251+4cos⁡(t)+4cos2⁡(t)+16sin2⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have

dxdt=ddt(t+2sin⁡(t))=1+2cos⁡(t) and dydt=ddt(1+cos⁡(2t))=−2sin⁡(2t).

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫25(1+2cos⁡(t))2+(−2sin⁡(2t))2dt=∫251+4cos⁡(t)+4cos2⁡(t)+4sin2⁡(2t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
content.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,y=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$
from $t=2$ to $t=5$ ?
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))=1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+4{cos}^{2}⁡(t)+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The derivatives are x′=3sin²(t)cos(t) and y′=−3cos²(t)sin(t). Using sin²(t)+cos²(t)=1, the speed simplifies to 3sin(t)cos(t) on [0,π/2]. Hence L=∫₀^{π/2}3sin(t)cos(t) dt=[(3/2)sin²(t)]₀^{π/2}=3/2, giving option d.

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,y={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{4}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={sin}^{3}⁡t,\,y={cos}^{3}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{3}⁡t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({cos}^{3}⁡t)=-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{4}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{4}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}(-1-1) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$ Substituting $\theta =\frac{t}{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{t}{2}) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & =-2\cdot 2\cdot {\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-4(0-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as x=t−sin⁡t,y=1−cos⁡t,t∈[0,π].

a
π2
b
2π
c
4
d
π
e
4π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the arc length L of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

Computing the derivatives of x and y, we have dxdt=ddt(t−sin⁡t)=1−cos⁡t and dydt=ddt(1−cos⁡t)=sin⁡t.

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get L=∫t1t2(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=∫0π(1−cos⁡t)2+(sin⁡t)2dt=∫0π1−2cos⁡t+cos2⁡t+sin2⁡tdt=∫0π2−2cos⁡tdt.

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, cos⁡(2θ)=1−2sin2⁡θ. Substituting θ=t2, we obtain

cos⁡(2⋅t2)=1−2sin2⁡(t2)cos⁡t=1−2sin2⁡(t2)1−cos⁡t=2sin2⁡(t2)2−2cos⁡t=4sin2⁡(t2)

Therefore,

∫0π2−2cos⁡tdt=∫0π4sin2⁡(t2)dt=2∫0πsin⁡(t2)dt=−2⋅2⋅cos⁡(t2)|0π=−4(cos⁡(π2)−cos⁡0)=−4(0−1)=4.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/ac040bc2c3eb943f947f34602c7c03e90f18e129a0fa7749d8ae60faaab12f71.png)

Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$
content.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the double-angle formula for cosine, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .$ Substituting $\theta =\frac{t}{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{t}{2}) & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2}) \\ 2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t & =4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & =-2\cdot 2\cdot {\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-4(0-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
